content.tldr: Encryption mathematically transforms plaintext into ciphertext using a cryptographic algorithm and key, while decryption reverses the process to recover original content.
content.simple_explanation: Encryption ensures confidentiality across untrusted storage and communication channels. In symmetric cryptography (e.g. AES-256), the exact same secret key encrypts and decrypts data, demanding secure out-of-band key exchange. In asymmetric cryptography (e.g. RSA, ECC), a mathematically linked key pair is used: a public key encrypts data that only the corresponding private key can decrypt, enabling secure communication between untrusted parties without pre-shared secrets.
content.real_world_example: A locked postal dispatch box: anyone with an open slot can drop a confidential letter inside the box, but only the authorized postal carrier possessing the physical key can open the rear door to retrieve and read the letters.
content.why_it_matters_and_pitfalls: Confidentiality alone does not guarantee message integrity or authenticity. Encrypting data without an Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) cipher like AES-GCM allows adversaries to tamper with ciphertext bits undetectable by the recipient.
